issue: Effect of court-sanctioned amalgamation on tenancy transfer and possible eviction or assignment consequences under Delhi rent control law
act: Delhi Rent Control Act, s. 14(1)(b), in the context of a court-sanctioned company amalgamation
date_scope: Judgment dated 5 December 1980; no broader historical version of the Rent Control Act is supplied
procedure_scope: Company scheme-sanction stage; the court states a prima facie view on vesting but expressly leaves eviction or actionable-assignment consequences for the appropriate rent-control or civil proceeding

conditions.text: Prima facie, contractual or statutory tenancy rights of the transferor company are transferable on amalgamation by the court's vesting order, without landlord consent, and fall outside s. 14(1)(b)
conditions.quote: Prima facie, the rights of the transferor-company in the tenancy, contractual or statutory, are transferable on an amalgamation by virtue of the vesting order to be made by the court while sanctioning the scheme of amalgamation or thereafter and having regard to the nature of such a vesting it would not require the consent of the landlord and would be outside the mischief of the provisions of s. 14(1)(b) of the Rent Control Act.

conditions.text: The court did not decide at this stage whether such transfer nevertheless amounts to an assignment that could support eviction under s. 14(1)(b) or a regular civil action
conditions.quote: This court is, however, not concerned at this stage if the transfer by or consequent on amalgamation by the order of the court would nevertheless be tantamount to the assignment of a tenancy and if without the consent of the landlord would render the company or the transferee-company liable to eviction under s. 14(1)(b) of the Rent Control Act or otherwise be actionable in a regular civil action against them.

conditions.text: Any such assignment or eviction question must be examined in the special jurisdiction created by the Rent Control Act or in a maintainable regular civil action
conditions.quote: Such a matter has to be examined and decided in accordance with the special jurisdiction created by that Act or on a regular civil action, if maintainable.

conditions.text: No landlord cause of action accrues before amalgamation and consequential vesting; any cause of action follows those events
conditions.quote: No cause of action accrues to the landlord before the amalgamation and consequential vesting. The cause of action, if any, follows the amalgamation and the vesting.

conditions.text: If an assignment in law attracts the Delhi Rent Control Act, the landlord remains free to proceed under that Act or by regular civil action before the appropriate authority
conditions.quote: If there is any assignment in law, which may attract the provisions of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the landlord would be free to take recourse to the proceedings under that Act or in a regular civil action and such proceedings would be dealt with and decided by the appropriate authority in accordance with law.

limitations: The source characterizes the tenancy-transfer proposition only as prima facie.
The core s. 14(1)(b) eviction or assignment question is expressly reserved and not finally adopted in this passage.

no

issue: Lawfulness and consent requirements for subletting or transfer of tenancy rights
act: Delhi Rent Control Act, section 16
date_scope: The supplied text distinguishes subletting before 9 June 1952, subletting on or after 9 June 1952, and conduct after commencement of the Act; the commencement date itself is not supplied.
procedure_scope: Substantive statutory treatment of subletting, assignment, and landlord consent; no target-case judicial interpretation is supplied.

conditions.text: A subletting made before 9 June 1952 is deemed lawful despite lack of landlord consent if the sub-tenant is in occupation at commencement of the Act.
conditions.quote: (1) Where at any time before the 9th day of June, 1952, a tenant has sub-let the whole or any part of the premises and the sub-tenant is, at the commencement of this Act, in occupation of such premises, then notwithstanding that the consent of the landlord was not obtained for such sub-letting, the premises shall be deemed to have been lawfully sub-let.

conditions.text: A subletting made on or after 9 June 1952 without the landlord's written consent is not deemed lawful.
conditions.quote: (2) No premises which have been sub-let either in whole or in part on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord, shall be deemed to have been lawfully sub-let.

conditions.text: After commencement of the Act, a tenant may neither sublet nor transfer or assign tenancy rights without the landlord's previous written consent.
conditions.quote: (3) After the commencement of this Act, no tenant shall, without the previous consent in writing of the landlord, -(a) sub-let the whole or any part of the premises held by him as a tenant; or(b) transfer or assign his rights in the tenancy or in any part thereof.

conditions.text: A landlord may not demand or receive a premium, pugree, or other consideration for consenting to subletting.
conditions.quote: (4) No landlord shall claim or receive the payment of any sum as premium or pugree or claim or receive any consideration whatsoever in cash or in kind for giving his consent to the sub-letting of the whole or any part of the premises held by the tenant.

issue: Partnership form, sham partnership, and retained control in subletting analysis
act: Goa rent statute; exact title is not stated in the supplied passage
date_scope: No specific temporal threshold is stated in the supplied passage.
procedure_scope: Supreme Court of India synthesis of subletting principles in a Goa rent-statute case, including Delhi precedents.

conditions.text: Inducting a business or professional partner by itself does not amount to subletting.
conditions.quote: Inducting a partner or partners in the business or profession by a tenant by itself does not amount to subletting.

conditions.quote: if the purpose of such partnership is ostensible and a deed of partnership is drawn to conceal the real transaction of sub-letting, the court may tear the veil of partnership to find out the real nature of transaction entered into by the tenant.

conditions.text: A partnership deed or other ostensible form does not bar the landlord from proving subletting or parting with possession through evidence or cross-examination.
conditions.quote: The existence of deed of partnership between tenant and alleged sub-tenant or ostensible transaction in any other form would not preclude the landlord from bringing on record material and circumstances, by adducing evidence or by means of cross-examination, making out a case of sub-letting or parting with possession in tenancy premises by the tenant in favour of a third person.

conditions.text: If the tenant remains actively associated with the partnership business and retains control over the tenancy premises, including jointly with partners, the tenant may not have parted with possession.
conditions.quote: If tenant is actively associated with the partnership business and retains the control over the tenancy premises with him, may be along with partners, the tenant may not be said to have parted with possession.

limitations: These are analogical principles from a Goa rent-statute case, not a statement that the Goa statute is Delhi substantive law.

issue: Pleading variance and proof of subletting concealed by an ostensible partnership

issue: Elements and burden shifting for proving subletting
act: Goa rent statute; exact title is not stated in the supplied passage

conditions.text: One ingredient of subletting is parting with all or part of the tenancy in favor of a third party with an exclusive right of possession.

issue: Lease-versus-license classification using written terms, exclusive possession, and retained control

But it is not a necessary inference of law that the occupier of an apartment in a hotel is not a tenant. Where, as in this case, the hotel-keeper retains no control over the apart- ment, the occupier is in the position of a tenant.

issue: Whether a court-confirmed liquidator transfer falls within assignment or parting with possession under section 14(1)(b)

conditions.text: The official liquidator stepped into the shoes of the original tenant, and a transfer under court orders was still made on behalf of that original tenant.
conditions.quote: the official liquidator had merely stepped into the shoes of Laxmi Bank which was the original tenant and even if the official liquidator had transferred the tenancy interest to respondent No.2 under the orders of the Court, it was on behalf of the original tenant.

conditions.text: The liquidator sale fell within section 14(1)(b) as a voluntary sale; even assuming it was involuntary, it was an assignment within section 14(b).
conditions.quote: It was undoubtedly a voluntary sale which clearly fell within the mischief of cite17†Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent control Act. Assuming that the sale by the official Liquidator was an involuntary sale, then it undoubtedly become an assignment as provided for by cite11†s.14(b) of Delhi Rent Control Act.

conditions.text: Section 14(b) is broad enough to include sublease, assignment, and other modes of parting with possession, including an involuntary sale in the authority quoted and adopted.
conditions.quote:
The language of s.14(b) is wide enough not only to include any sub-
lease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted. In view of the wide amplitude of s.14(b) we are clearly of the opinion that it does not exclude even an involuntary sale.

a subtenant is given a special right, not available to him under the general law, but that right is circumscribed by specific conditions laid down in section

issue: Heritability of commercial tenancy and business after the tenant's death
act: Delhi Rent Control Act
date_scope: Applies to succession on death of a commercial tenant, including where the contractual tenancy had previously been terminated.
procedure_scope: Supreme Court of India determination of succession and continued statutory protection for heirs of a commercial tenant.

conditions.text: While the contractual tenancy of a commercial tenant continues, the deceased tenant's heirs inherit both the tenancy and the business and may run and enjoy the business.
conditions.quote: So long as the contractual tenancy of a tenant who carries on the business continues, there can be no question of the heirs of the deceased tenant not only inheriting the tenancy but also inheriting the business and they are entitled to run and enjoy the same.

conditions.text: Mere termination of contractual tenancy does not change the tenant's statutory status unless the Rent Act provides otherwise.
conditions.quote: mere termination of the contractual tenancy does not bring about any change in the status of the tenant and the tenant by virtue of the definition of the `tenant' in the Act and the other Rent Acts continues to enjoy the same status and position unless there be any provisions in the Rent Acts which indicate to the contrary.

conditions.text: For commercial premises under the Delhi Act, the absence of a statutory restriction leaves ordinary inheritance applicable, and heirs succeed to both tenancy rights and the business as a whole.
conditions.quote: the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard to succession. It may also be borne in mind that in case of commercial premises the heirs of the deceased tenant not only succeed to the tenancy rights in the premises but they succeed to the business as a whole.

conditions.text: Commercial tenancies therefore devolve on heirs despite determination of the contractual tenancy; heirs retain Act protection and may be evicted only in accordance with the Act.
conditions.quote: commercial tenancies notwithstanding the determination of the contractual tenancies will devolve on the heirs in accordance with law and the heirs who step into the position of the deceased tenant will continue to enjoy the protection afforded by the Act and they can only be evicted in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

limitations: The passage concerns death and inheritance of commercial tenancy; residential statutory limitations and corporate amalgamation are different subjects.
Later legal changes are not audited in the supplied material; the source is retrospective and incomplete.
